_readme: Cleansing & exfoliating product pack for the K-beauty library, consumed by build-kbeauty-pages.cjs (kbeauty-products-*.json). Descriptions are written from public product information. Cosmetic structure-function wording only, no invented INCI lists, no invented percentages, no prices stated where uncertain.

products.name: Heartleaf Pore Control Cleansing Oil
products.whatItIs: The product that turned Anua from a small Korean label into an export brand. It is a first-step cleansing oil built around 어성초 (eoseongcho), the heartleaf extract the brand uses across its range, in a light ester base rather than a heavy mineral or plant oil. It goes on thin, dissolves sunscreen and long-wear base makeup quickly, and emulsifies into a milky wash instead of leaving a slick. The pore-control framing is marketing; the cleansing performance is the real reason it sold.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin that wants makeup and SPF off without a greasy after-feel. It suits congestion-prone skin better than most balms because the texture is light and rinses fully rather than sitting in the folds around the nose. Very dry skin may find it leaves nothing behind and prefer a richer balm. Check the current ingredient list for fragrance before buying if you react easily.
products.howToUse: First step of an evening 이중 세안 (ijung sean) double cleanse. Two or three pumps onto dry hands and a dry face, massage for around a minute so it can break down sunscreen and makeup, then add a splash of water and keep working until it turns milky. Rinse lukewarm and follow with a water-based cleanser. PM only.
products.watchOut: The blackhead angle is doing heavy lifting. An oil cleanser can loosen surface plugs and stop new ones setting; it does not empty pores, and nothing you rinse off in sixty seconds will. The other common complaint is a slippery film afterwards, which almost always means it was not emulsified properly — add more water and massage longer rather than skipping the second cleanse.

products.name: Clean It Zero Cleansing Balm Original
products.korean: 클린 잇 제로 클렌징 밤 오리지널
products.whatItIs: The balm that made cleansing balms a category outside Korea. A sherbet-textured solid that melts on contact with warm skin, breaks down makeup, sunscreen and sebum, then emulsifies with water into a milk you rinse away. There is no headline active and the brand does not really claim one — the whole product is texture, reliability and a spatula. It has been on shelves long enough to be one of the most thoroughly reviewed cleansers in K-beauty, which counts for something.
products.whoItSuits: Almost everyone, which is exactly why it sells. Dry and normal skin get a comfortable first cleanse that does not strip; anyone wearing base makeup or a proper layer of sunscreen gets a thoroughness gel cleansers cannot match. Oily and blemish-prone skin often prefers the Purifying version. If you wear waterproof mascara daily, a balm like this is the most useful single addition to a routine.
products.howToUse: Scoop with the spatula rather than wet fingers, and work roughly a large blueberry's worth into completely dry skin for thirty to sixty seconds. Add water a little at a time and massage until the balm turns white and milky, then rinse lukewarm and follow with a water-based cleanser. Evening only — there is nothing to dissolve at 7am.
products.watchOut: It is fragranced and the scent is noticeable. The bigger practical problem is under-emulsifying: if you do not add enough water, a film stays behind and can read as congestion, so people who think they break out from balms are often just under-rinsing. Keep the jar out of shower steam, which softens the sherbet into a puddle you cannot scoop.

products.name: Clean It Zero Cleansing Balm Purifying
products.whatItIs: The variant of Clean It Zero aimed at oily and blemish-prone skin. Same sherbet-balm mechanism as the Original — melt on dry skin, emulsify with water, rinse — with a lighter finish and a botanical angle rather than the comfort-first slant of the pink one. Think of the line as one product in several finishes: the differences between the variants are real but modest, and the choice comes down to how your skin feels an hour after rinsing.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin that likes the convenience of a balm but finds the Original leaves things a little too cushioned. Also a sensible pick if you wear sunscreen daily and want it properly off without a foaming cleanser doing all the work. Dry or reactive skin will usually be happier with the Original, which is more comfortable and less brisk on the rinse.
products.howToUse: Dry hands, dry face, a spatula scoop massaged in for around a minute so it has time to break down sunscreen and makeup. Add water gradually until it emulsifies to a milk, rinse lukewarm, then follow with a gentle water-based cleanser. Evening only, and once a day is plenty even if your skin is oily.
products.watchOut: "Purifying" is a cosmetic word, not a treatment claim — this is a cleanser, and it will not clear breakouts. It is still fragranced, so reactive skin gains nothing by choosing this variant over the Original. And because oily skin often over-cleanses, resist the urge to use a balm morning and night; stripping oil tends to provoke more of it.

products.name: All Clean Balm
products.whatItIs: A shea-rich sherbet balm that became the default budget alternative to Clean It Zero and has arguably outlasted the comparison. It is noticeably more buttery than most balms, which is the point: it melts slowly, gives you a long working time to break down eye makeup, and leaves skin feeling cushioned rather than squeaky. It emulsifies cleanly for a formula this rich. Sold in a jar with a spatula and, more usefully, in a travel tube.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, flaky and winter-tight skin, and anyone whose skin feels stripped by lighter cleansing oils. It is gentle enough around the eyes for most people, which matters if you wear waterproof mascara. Oily skin can use it but often finds the shea content leaves more behind than it wants — a lighter ester-based oil suits that skin better as a first step.
products.howToUse: Take a scoop with the spatula onto dry hands, warm it briefly, and massage into dry skin for around a minute, spending longer over eye makeup. Add lukewarm water gradually and keep massaging until it turns milky, then rinse and follow with a water-based cleanser. PM only, once daily.
products.watchOut: Rich balms need a proper second cleanse — skip it and the shea can leave a film that oily and congestion-prone skin will notice within a few days. It carries a herbal-citrus scent that some people find strong. And the jar format is a hygiene consideration: use the spatula, not fingers, and do not leave it open in a steamy bathroom.

products.name: Radiance Cleansing Balm
products.whatItIs: A sherbet balm built around rice bran oil, keeping Beauty of Joseon's hanbang framing consistent across the range. It melts fast, has a slightly thinner working texture than the shea-heavy balms, and emulsifies without much coaxing. The radiance in the name comes from a clean, well-hydrated surface after a thorough first cleanse — it is not a brightening product, and the brand is reasonably honest about that on the pack.
products.whoItSuits: Normal to dry skin that wants a comfortable first cleanse without a heavy after-feel, and anyone already using the brand's Relief Sun sunscreen who wants something that reliably removes it. Combination skin gets on with it well. If your main concern is oiliness or active congestion, a lighter oil rinses more completely and will serve you better as a nightly first step.
products.howToUse: Spatula a scoop onto dry hands, work into dry skin for thirty to sixty seconds, then add water and emulsify to a milk before rinsing. Follow with a water-based cleanser. Evening only. If you have worn a mineral or heavily water-resistant sunscreen, give it the full minute rather than rushing.
products.watchOut: Do not read "radiance" as brightening — nothing that leaves your face in under two minutes will shift pigmentation, and this contains no meaningful brightening actives. The jar is small for the price once you account for how much a proper first cleanse uses, and like all jar balms it wants a spatula and a dry bathroom shelf rather than the ledge inside the shower.

products.name: Cleansing Oil & Blackhead PHA
products.whatItIs: A cleansing oil with PHA (gluconolactone) folded into the formula, which is an interesting idea more than a proven one. The oil base itself is genuinely good: light, quick to emulsify, and effective on sunscreen and long-wear makeup without the residue heavier oils leave. The acid is best understood as an extra rather than the reason to buy. It is one of the longer-established Korean cleansing oils sold internationally.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin dealing with visible blackheads around the nose and chin who want their first cleanse to feel light. It works well as a daily makeup-and-SPF remover for most skin types that are not actively dry. If your skin is dry or reactive, the acid content is not a problem in itself, but you will likely prefer a balm for comfort.
products.howToUse: Pump onto dry skin, massage for around a minute concentrating on congested areas, add water to emulsify, then rinse and follow with a water-based cleanser. PM only. There is no benefit to leaving it on longer in the hope the acid does more — it will not, and prolonged massage irritates more than it clears.
products.watchOut: The PHA is the marketing hook and the weakest part of the pitch. Acids need contact time to do anything measurable, and a cleanser sits on your face for a minute before being rinsed away. Treat any smoothing you notice as a bonus, not a reason to skip a leave-on exfoliant. If texture is your primary concern, a BHA liquid is the product that actually addresses it.

products.name: Gentle Black Deep Cleansing Oil
products.whatItIs: One of the older cleansing oils in the international K-beauty catalogue, built on a blend of dark-coloured plant oils — black bean, black sesame and black currant seed among them — which is where the name comes from rather than any charcoal or clay. It is thicker than the current generation of ester-based oils, gives a slow, comfortable massage, and emulsifies to a soft milk. Klairs has kept it largely unchanged for years.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, normal and sensitive skin that finds newer lightweight oils too quick and stripping. The heavier plant-oil base is comfortable on skin that feels tight after cleansing, and it removes eye makeup patiently. Oily and congestion-prone skin will probably find it too rich for nightly use and should look at a lighter emulsifying oil instead.
products.howToUse: Two to three pumps onto dry skin, massaged for a full minute so the plant oils have time to loosen makeup and sunscreen. Add lukewarm water and emulsify thoroughly before rinsing. Always follow with a water-based cleanser. PM only, once a day — richer oils reward patience more than repetition.
products.watchOut: Plant-oil-heavy formulas need a genuinely thorough second cleanse; this is the kind of oil that leaves a faint film if you rush, and that film is what people mistake for a reaction. It has a distinct nutty-herbal smell that not everyone likes. Those with fungal acne concerns should note that plant oil blends are the category most often implicated, though the evidence on any individual formula is thin.

products.name: Madagascar Centella Light Cleansing Oil
products.whatItIs: SKIN1004's cleansing oil, carrying the same Madagascan-sourced centella framing as the ampoule that made the brand. The word Light in the name is accurate — it is one of the thinner cleansing oils on the market, closer to a fluid than an oil, and it emulsifies almost immediately. Centella in a rinse-off product is a mild gesture rather than a treatment, but the base itself is well made and unfussy.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive and blemish-prone skin that wants the double-cleanse step without a rich texture sitting on the face. Good for oily and combination skin, and a reasonable choice for people new to oil cleansing who are nervous about congestion. If you wear heavy or waterproof makeup, a proper balm removes it more completely in one pass.
products.howToUse: Two pumps onto dry skin, massage for thirty to sixty seconds, add water to emulsify and rinse. Follow with a gentle water-based cleanser. PM only. Because it is so light, most people find they need a touch more product than with a balm — using too little is the usual reason it seems not to work.
products.watchOut: Do not expect the centella to calm anything. 진정 (jinjeong), the soothing effect Korean brands market so heavily, requires the ingredient to stay on the skin; a cleanser is rinsed off long before that can matter. The formula is also on the thin side for heavy base makeup and stubborn mineral sunscreen — you may find yourself doing two rounds, which defeats the economy.

products.name: Cleanse Me Softly Milk Cleanser
products.whatItIs: A low-pH milk cleanser from a small Korean brand built around seasonally harvested plant ingredients. Milk cleansers occupy an odd middle ground — richer than a gel, lighter than a balm — and this one leans firmly towards gentleness. It removes light makeup and sunscreen, rinses without squeak, and is one of the few cleansers that genuinely suits skin in the middle of a barrier flare-up. It has quietly become the brand's signature product internationally.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, sensitive and over-exfoliated skin that finds every foaming cleanser leaves it tight. Also useful as a morning cleanser for people who do not want to foam at all. It is not the right tool if you wear full base makeup or heavily water-resistant sunscreen — a balm or oil handles those, with this as the second step or a lighter-day alternative.
products.howToUse: Apply to dry or barely damp skin, massage gently for around thirty seconds, then rinse with lukewarm water. Usable morning and evening. In the evening, if you have worn makeup or a substantial sunscreen, use an oil or balm first and treat this as the water-based follow-up rather than the whole cleanse.
products.watchOut: The seasonal-harvest, fresh-ingredient story is brand identity, not evidence — nothing about a plant being picked at a particular time changes how a cleanser performs. Practically, it is under-powered for heavy makeup, and the milk texture leaves a slight slip that some people mistake for residue. Rinse a little longer than instinct suggests and that impression usually goes.

products.name: Low pH Good Morning Gel Cleanser
products.whatItIs: The cleanser that taught a generation of readers what cleanser pH means. It is a mildly acidic gel that foams lightly, includes a small amount of BHA and tea tree oil, and rinses without the tight squeak of a traditional alkaline foaming wash. Its importance is historical as much as practical: it made low-pH cleansing a mainstream expectation. As a daily gel cleanser it remains competent, cheap and widely available.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin that wants a morning cleanse which does not strip, and anyone whose skin has been irritated by high-pH foaming washes. It is a reasonable second cleanse in the evening too. Dry and very sensitive skin may still find it slightly brisk and be happier with a milk or cream cleanser, particularly in winter.
products.howToUse: A small amount on damp skin, massaged for around thirty seconds, then rinsed lukewarm. Fine morning and evening. In the evening use it after an oil or balm rather than instead of one. There is no benefit to leaving it sitting on the face — the low pH is about how it rinses, not about doing something while it waits.
products.watchOut: The BHA content is far too low, and the contact time far too short, for this to affect breakouts — a lot of people bought it as an acne treatment because of the ingredient list and were disappointed. It is a good gentle cleanser, nothing more. It also contains tea tree oil, which a small number of people react to, so patch-test if essential oils have caused you trouble before.

products.name: Salicylic Acid Daily Gentle Cleanser
products.whatItIs: A foaming gel cleanser aimed at blemish-prone skin, with salicylic acid and tea tree in a formula that still rinses at a skin-friendly pH. It foams more than the Low pH Good Morning cleanser and feels more decisive on oily skin, which is why people with congestion tend to prefer it. Like most acid cleansers, its value lies in being a non-stripping daily wash rather than in the acid itself.
products.whoItSuits: Oily, congested and blemish-prone skin that wants something more substantial than a low-foam gel without going back to a stripping bar. Works as an evening second cleanse and, for very oily skin, a morning wash. Dry, sensitive or currently over-exfoliated skin should skip it — there is nothing here it needs, and the foaming will not help.
products.howToUse: Half a pump on damp skin, worked into a light foam and massaged for about thirty seconds before rinsing. Evening as the second step after an oil or balm; morning only if your skin genuinely runs oily. Once daily is enough for most people. Follow with moisturiser, and with sunscreen in the morning.
products.watchOut: Salicylic acid in a cleanser is one of the most over-sold ideas in skincare. It is rinsed away in under a minute, at a concentration and pH set for a wash rather than a treatment, so it cannot replace a leave-on BHA. Using it twice daily in the hope of speeding things up mostly produces dryness, which prompts more oil — the opposite of the goal.

products.name: Green Plum Refreshing Cleanser
products.whatItIs: A low-pH gel cleanser built on green plum (매실, maesil), a Korean fruit with a long culinary history that the brand uses for its hanbang framing. It is a modest, well-behaved daily cleanser: light foam, quick rinse, no tightness afterwards. Nothing about it is remarkable, which is arguably the point — it fills the second-cleanse slot cheaply and consistently, and it pairs naturally with the rest of the range.
products.whoItSuits: Combination and normal skin looking for an everyday second cleanse that does not strip, and people building a first routine who want the low-pH box ticked without overthinking it. Oily skin will find it adequate but not bracing. If you have dry or reactive skin, a milk or cream cleanser is a more comfortable choice than any gel, including this one.
products.howToUse: A small amount on damp skin, lathered lightly in the hands first, massaged for around thirty seconds and rinsed with lukewarm water. Suitable morning and evening. At night, use it after an oil cleanser or balm rather than on its own if you have worn makeup or a substantial layer of sunscreen.
products.watchOut: Green plum is a story rather than an active — there is no meaningful evidence that it does anything measurable in a rinse-off product, and the brand does not really claim otherwise. It has a light scent that reactive skin should note. If you want a cleanser doing actual work, the honest answer is that no cleanser does much beyond cleaning without irritating.

products.name: 1025 Dokdo Cleanser
products.whatItIs: The companion to Round Lab's 1025 Dokdo Toner, one of the most consistently recommended everyday cleansers in Korea. It is a low-pH gel that foams softly and rinses clean, built on the brand's deep-sea mineral water framing from the waters around 독도 (Dokdo). The formula is deliberately unexciting: no acids, no strong actives, no scent to speak of. That restraint is why it works as a daily wash for most people.
products.whoItSuits: Combination, normal and mildly sensitive skin that wants something dependable twice a day. It is a particularly good default for people whose skin has been irritated by stronger cleansers and who need a reset. Very dry skin may still want a cream or milk cleanser in winter, and skin with heavy congestion will not find any treatment benefit here.
products.howToUse: A short strip on damp skin, worked to a light lather and massaged for around thirty seconds, then rinsed lukewarm. Morning and evening. In the evening, use it as the second step after an oil or balm if you have worn sunscreen or makeup. Follow with toner while the skin is still damp.
products.watchOut: Deep-sea mineral water is marketing. There is no good evidence that mineral content in a rinse-off cleanser changes anything about skin, and the brand's whole identity leans on the idea. Judge the product on what it actually is — a mild, low-pH, fragrance-light daily gel — and it holds up well. Judge it on the Dokdo story and you are paying for geography.

products.name: SoonJung pH 6.5 Whip Cleanser
products.whatItIs: The cleanser from Etude's 순정 (SoonJung) line, which the brand built specifically around minimal-ingredient formulas for reactive skin. Panthenol and madecassoside are the named soothing components, and the pH is set close to skin's own. The whip in the name refers to the texture: it emerges as a soft cream and works into a very low, dense foam rather than a squeaky lather. Widely available and cheap.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive, easily flushed and over-exfoliated skin that reacts to almost everything else. It is one of the safest cleansers to recommend blind, and a sensible morning wash for dry skin. Oily and congested skin can use it but will likely find it too mild to feel like it has done anything, which is a perception problem more than a performance one.
products.howToUse: A small amount on damp skin, massaged for twenty to thirty seconds and rinsed lukewarm. Morning and evening. At night, use an oil or balm first if you have worn makeup or a real layer of sunscreen; this is not designed to shift either on its own. Follow immediately with toner or moisturiser.
products.watchOut: It barely foams, and people used to a squeaky finish often decide it is not working and scrub harder or double-wash — which undoes the entire point of a gentle cleanser. The soothing ingredients are rinsed off, so do not expect them to calm anything; the benefit is in what the formula leaves out, not what it adds. Very oily skin may genuinely need something stronger.

products.name: Low pH Pore Deep Cleansing Foam
products.whatItIs: Pyunkang Yul's daily foaming cleanser, in keeping with a brand whose whole approach is short ingredient lists and no theatre. It produces a proper dense foam — more than the low-pH gels — while staying mildly acidic, which is a harder balance to strike than it sounds. The pore claim refers to how thoroughly it clears surface oil, not to any resurfacing action. Good value, plain packaging, no fragrance to speak of.
products.whoItSuits: Combination and oily skin that wants the satisfaction of a real lather without the tightness that usually comes with it. Works as an evening second cleanse for most skin types. Dry and sensitive skin will probably find it more than they need — a low-foam gel or a milk cleanser is kinder, particularly in cold weather.
products.howToUse: A small amount lathered in wet hands first, then massaged over damp skin for around thirty seconds and rinsed lukewarm. Evening as the second step after an oil or balm; morning only if your skin is genuinely oily on waking. Follow with hydrating toner while skin is still damp rather than after it has dried.
products.watchOut: Foam is not evidence. A dense lather feels thorough, but it also makes it easy to over-cleanse, and oily skin that strips itself twice daily usually produces more oil in response. "Pore deep" is a claim no rinse-off cleanser can support — pores are not emptied by washing. Use it once a day and judge by how your skin feels an hour later.

products.name: Yam Root Vegan Milk Cleanser
products.whatItIs: A low-pH milk cleanser built around yam root (마, ma), an ingredient chosen for its viscous, mucilaginous texture as much as anything else. It behaves like a cream cleanser: no foam, a slippery massage, and a rinse that leaves skin soft rather than squeaky. Isntree formulates it without animal-derived ingredients. It sits in the same niche as the brand's hydration range — comfort first, actives elsewhere in the routine.
products.whoItSuits: Dry, dehydrated and sensitive skin, and anyone whose barrier is currently unhappy from too much exfoliation. A good morning cleanser for skin that does not want to foam before breakfast. Oily and congested skin usually finds milk cleansers unsatisfying and will get on better with a low-pH gel or a light foam.
products.howToUse: Apply to dry or lightly damp skin, massage for around thirty seconds, then rinse thoroughly with lukewarm water. Morning and evening. In the evening treat it as the second step after an oil or balm if you have worn makeup or sunscreen — a milk cleanser alone will not clear a water-resistant SPF.
products.watchOut: The slip is the main complaint: milk cleansers leave a soft, faintly coated feeling that people read as residue and respond to by washing again, which defeats the purpose. Rinse a little longer instead. The vegan formulation is an ethical claim rather than a performance one, and yam root has no meaningful evidence behind it beyond providing the texture.

products.name: AHA-BHA-PHA 30 Days Miracle Acne Clear Foam
products.whatItIs: The cleanser from the set that made Some By Mi a household name in blemish-focused K-beauty. It combines all three acid families with tea tree in a foaming wash, and it is usually bought alongside the matching toner and serum. As a cleanser it is a competent, brisk foam for oily skin. The 30-day framing belongs to the marketing of the range as a whole rather than to anything this particular product does.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and blemish-prone skin that wants a decisive evening wash and is already using proper leave-on treatment elsewhere. It is a reasonable second cleanse after an oil or balm. Dry, sensitive or currently irritated skin should stay away — three acid types plus tea tree in a foaming base is more provocation than benefit for reactive skin.
products.howToUse: A small amount lathered in wet hands, massaged over damp skin for about thirty seconds, rinsed lukewarm. Evening, after an oil cleanser. Once daily is enough. If you are also using a leave-on exfoliant, consider alternating nights rather than stacking both, and always follow with moisturiser.
products.watchOut: The name promises a timeline no cleanser can deliver, and the acids are rinsed away long before they can act — this is not a treatment, whatever the packaging implies. The bigger risk is the full set: using acid cleanser, acid toner and acid serum together is a well-trodden route to a stripped, stinging barrier. Persistent or painful breakouts are a matter for a doctor, not a foam.

products.name: DIVE-IN Low Molecular Hyaluronic Acid Cleansing Foam
products.whatItIs: The cleanser in Torriden's DIVE-IN range, the vegan hydration line built on low-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid that carries the brand internationally. It is a mild, low-foaming wash designed to leave skin feeling cushioned rather than clean-squeaky, with no fragrance in the formula. As with every cleanser in this bracket, the appeal is in what it avoids doing: it does not strip, and it does not leave a film.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and dehydrated skin, and anyone using the rest of the DIVE-IN range who wants consistency across the routine. It is gentle enough for most sensitive skin. Oily and congested skin will find it perfectly usable but underwhelming — there is no oil-control angle here, and nothing addressing blackheads.
products.howToUse: A short amount on damp skin, lathered lightly and massaged for around thirty seconds before rinsing with lukewarm water. Morning and evening. Follow immediately with a hydrating toner while the skin is still damp — that is where the hyaluronic acid in this routine actually earns its keep.
products.watchOut: Hyaluronic acid in a rinse-off product is close to decorative. It is a humectant that works by staying on the skin and holding water there; wash it away and the benefit goes with it. The naming across the range invites you to think the cleanser hydrates in the way the serum does. It does not — it simply avoids drying you out, which is a lower and more honest bar.

products.name: Heartleaf Quercetinol Pore Deep Cleansing Foam
products.whatItIs: The second-cleanse partner to Anua's cleansing oil, keeping heartleaf as the through-line. It is a low-pH foaming cleanser with a soft, dense lather that rinses without tightness — brisker than the gentlest gels, milder than a traditional foam. Quercetinol is the brand's coined term for its heartleaf-derived complex rather than a standardised ingredient, so read it as branding. The cleansing performance is the part that stands up.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin that wants a proper wash after an oil cleanse, especially anyone already using the Heartleaf oil and toner and wanting the range to hang together. It suits blemish-prone skin reasonably well. Dry and sensitive skin will do better with a milk or cream cleanser — the foam is mild, but it is still a foam.
products.howToUse: A small amount worked into a lather in wet hands, massaged over damp skin for around thirty seconds, rinsed lukewarm. Evening as the second step after the oil cleanser; morning too if your skin is oily on waking. Follow with a hydrating toner on damp skin rather than waiting for the face to dry.
products.watchOut: "Quercetinol" sounds like a defined active and is not — it is a brand name for a heartleaf extract complex, and no rinse-off product delivers a soothing ingredient in a way that lasts. "Pore deep" is the same over-claim every cleanser in this category makes. Judge it as a good mild foam at a fair price, and put your money into a leave-on product if pores are the concern.

products.name: Rich Moist Foaming Cleanser
products.whatItIs: A long-established low-pH cream-to-foam cleanser aimed at dry and comfort-seeking skin. It produces a soft, small-bubble lather rather than a squeaky one, and it is formulated without added fragrance, which is why it turns up so often in recommendations for reactive skin. Klairs has kept the formula stable for years, and it is one of the few gentle foaming cleansers with a genuinely long track record on the international market.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and sensitive skin that still wants the ritual of a foaming wash without the tight, stripped after-feel. A sound morning cleanser and a reliable second cleanse at night. Oily and heavily congested skin will find it too soft to feel like it has done the job and will be better served by a brisker low-pH foam.
products.howToUse: Lather a small amount in wet hands, massage over damp skin for twenty to thirty seconds, and rinse lukewarm. Morning and evening. At night, use after an oil or balm if you have worn makeup or sunscreen. Apply toner or moisturiser while the skin is still slightly damp for the best comfort.
products.watchOut: It is not powerful enough to remove a water-resistant sunscreen on its own — plenty of people use it as a single evening cleanse and wonder why their skin looks congested a fortnight later. "Rich moist" describes how it feels during and after washing, not a moisturising benefit that persists. Any cleanser's job is to leave without a trace, and this one does exactly that.

products.name: Sunday Morning Refreshing Cleansing Foam
products.whatItIs: Axis-Y's everyday foaming cleanser, following the brand's habit of naming products after a mood rather than an ingredient. It is a low-pH foam with a light, quick lather and a clean rinse, positioned as the mild daily wash that sits under the brand's better-known dark-spot serum. Nothing about the formula is unusual; the appeal is that it is a competent gentle foam from a range people already trust.
products.whoItSuits: Combination and normal skin looking for an unfussy twice-daily cleanser, and existing Axis-Y users who want the routine to come from one place. Oily skin will find it adequate as a second cleanse. Dry and sensitive skin should look at a milk or cream cleanser instead — this is mild but it is still a foaming surfactant wash.
products.howToUse: Lather a small amount in wet hands, work over damp skin for about thirty seconds and rinse with lukewarm water. Morning and evening, using an oil or balm first at night if you have worn makeup or sunscreen. Follow with toner on damp skin. One pea-sized amount is plenty; more foam does not mean more clean.
products.watchOut: There is no reason to seek this out specifically — it is a good cleanser in a category full of good cleansers, and it costs a little more than several equally capable Korean foams. Buy it because you like the rest of the range rather than because it does something the others do not. Nothing in a cleanser at this price is going to address dullness or pores in any lasting way.

products.name: Gentle Cleansing Foam
products.whatItIs: The cleanser from Sulwhasoo's 순행 (Sunhaeng) line, the entry point into a brand otherwise built on ginseng-led prestige serums and creams. It is a dense, creamy foam with the hanbang herbal scent the house is known for, and it rinses without any tightness. As a piece of formulation it is well made and pleasant. As a purchase it is a luxury-tier price for a step that lasts under a minute.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and mature skin that treats cleansing as part of the pleasure of a routine and wants the scent and texture to match the rest of a Sulwhasoo shelf. It is genuinely comfortable and does not strip. If you are choosing between spending on this or on a treatment step, the treatment step is where the money does more.
products.howToUse: Lather a small amount in wet hands, massage over damp skin for around thirty seconds, then rinse with lukewarm water. Evening as the second cleanse after an oil or balm; morning if your skin tolerates a foam on waking. Follow with the first essence or toner while skin is still damp.
products.watchOut: This is the clearest example in the category of paying for a rinse-off. No cleanser, at any price, stays on the skin long enough for expensive botanicals to matter; the herbal scent is real and the formula is comfortable, but so are cleansers at a fifth of the cost. The fragrance is also pronounced, which rules it out for anyone whose skin flares at scent.

products.name: Volcanic Pore Cleansing Foam
products.whatItIs: Part of Innisfree's long-running Jeju volcanic range, built on 화산송이 (hwasansongi), the porous volcanic clay from the island that the brand has used since the line launched. The cleanser combines that clay with a foaming base, producing a brisk lather and a distinctly matte finish. It is one of the oldest surviving products in international K-beauty and remains the default recommendation for very oily skin in Korean drugstores.
products.whoItSuits: Genuinely oily skin — the sort that is shining by lunchtime — and combination skin that needs a firmer hand on the T-zone in summer. It suits congestion-prone skin as an evening second cleanse. Dry, sensitive or dehydrated skin should avoid it outright; the matte finish that oily skin enjoys is the same thing dry skin experiences as tightness.
products.howToUse: Lather a small amount in wet hands and massage over damp skin for about thirty seconds, concentrating on the T-zone rather than the cheeks, then rinse lukewarm. Evening after an oil cleanser. Once daily unless your skin is very oily. Follow with a lightweight moisturiser — skipping it because you feel matte is a mistake.
products.watchOut: Clay plus foaming surfactant is an efficient way to strip, and stripped oily skin reliably produces more oil. The pore claim is the usual over-reach: volcanic clay absorbs surface sebum, it does not clear anything from inside a pore. If your skin feels tight or looks flaky after a few weeks, that is the formula working too hard, not your skin needing more cleansing.

products.name: Treatment Enzyme Peel
products.whatItIs: A powder cleanser and enzyme exfoliant, and one of the most copied product formats to come out of Korea. The powder activates when you add water in your palm, foaming into a soft lather while enzymes work on the surface layer of dead cells. It is a considered, well-engineered version of a format that is now everywhere. Powder also solves a real problem: it needs no preservative load and travels without leaking.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and dry skin dealing with a rough or dull surface that finds acids too provoking. Enzyme exfoliation is milder than acid exfoliation and easier to fit alongside retinoids, so it suits people already running an active routine. Very oily or heavily congested skin will get more from a BHA. It is usable on sensitive skin, but start once a week.
products.howToUse: Tip a small amount of powder into a wet palm, add water, and work into a lather before massaging over damp skin for thirty to sixty seconds. Rinse lukewarm. Two or three times a week in the evening, in place of your usual second cleanse — not in addition to it. Never on the same night as a leave-on acid or retinoid.
products.watchOut: Enzyme exfoliation has less evidence behind it than acids, and the effect is subtle rather than transformative — anyone expecting resurfacing will be underwhelmed for the money. The bigger risk is habit: powder cleansers feel so mild that people use them daily, which quietly over-exfoliates. And the sensation of instant smoothness after any exfoliant is mostly water in the surface layer, not new skin.

products.name: Brightening Peeling Gel
products.whatItIs: A peeling gel — the format where a clear gel is massaged onto dry skin and rolls up into greyish pills you rinse away. Dr.G's is among the best-known internationally and one of the gentler ones. It is worth being clear about the mechanism: the pills are mostly the gel-forming polymer clumping under friction, mixed with a little surface debris. The exfoliation comes from the massage, not from anything dissolving.
products.whoItSuits: Normal, combination and dry skin that finds acid exfoliants stinging and wants something less demanding once or twice a week. It is a reasonable first exfoliant for a nervous beginner. Blemish-prone skin should be cautious — rubbing over active spots is not helpful. Anyone using retinoids or acids already does not need this on top.
products.howToUse: Apply to completely dry skin — any water and it will not pill — and massage gently in small circles for around thirty seconds. Rinse with lukewarm water and follow with a hydrating toner. Once or twice a week at most, in the evening. Never on the same night as a leave-on acid or retinoid, and never on broken or irritated skin.
products.watchOut: The satisfying grey rolls are largely the product, not your dead skin, and the visual is doing most of the persuading in this category. Because it looks so productive, people over-use it and end up with the tight, shiny, sensitised look of over-exfoliation. "Brightening" here means a smoother surface reflecting light, not any effect on pigmentation — for that you need a leave-on active and daily sunscreen.

products.name: Gentle Black Sugar Facial Polish
products.whatItIs: A sugar-based physical scrub in an oil-rich base, sitting in a category most of the industry has spent a decade moving away from. Klairs' version is unusually well made for what it is: the sugar granules dissolve as you work, so abrasion decreases rather than continuing, and the oil base cushions the massage. It is a nostalgic format done carefully rather than a modern exfoliating approach.
products.whoItSuits: Dry and flaky skin that wants a physical smoothing before makeup, and people who simply prefer a scrub and will not be talked into acids. The dissolving granules make it one of the safer options in the format. It is not for blemish-prone or sensitive skin, and not for anyone using retinoids, acids or a prescription treatment.
products.howToUse: Apply to dry skin and massage very lightly for around thirty seconds, letting the sugar dissolve — pressure is not the point and adds nothing. Rinse with lukewarm water and follow with a water-based cleanser to clear the oil base. Once a week in the evening at most. Follow with moisturiser and use sunscreen the next day.
products.watchOut: Physical scrubs are the exfoliation method with the weakest case: uneven abrasion, easy to over-do, and no meaningful advantage over a mild acid. The oil base also needs a proper second cleanse or it leaves a film. If you have active breakouts, dragging granules across inflamed skin is a genuinely bad idea — pick a leave-on BHA instead and leave scrubs to the elbows.

products.name: Chestnut BHA 2% Clear Liquid
products.whatItIs: A leave-on BHA liquid built on salicylic acid alongside chestnut shell extract, which is where the name comes from. Unlike an acid cleanser, this stays on the skin, which is the only way a BHA can do the thing BHAs are good at — working through sebum to loosen what is blocking a pore. Isntree keeps the formula plain and low-fragrance, in line with the rest of its range.
products.whoItSuits: Oily, congested and blackhead-prone skin, particularly around the nose, chin and forehead. It also helps the rough, bumpy texture that comes with persistent congestion. Dry and sensitive skin should approach carefully or choose a PHA instead. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, ask a doctor before adding any salicylic acid product to a routine.
products.howToUse: Evening, after cleansing and before heavier layers, on dry skin. Start two nights a week and build slowly — most people settle at three or four. Follow with a moisturiser, and wear sunscreen daily, which matters more with any exfoliant in the routine. Do not use it on the same night as a retinoid until you know how your skin behaves.
products.watchOut: Some stinging on application is common and not a sign it is working. The bigger issue is enthusiasm: nightly use from the start is the fastest route to a stripped, shiny, over-exfoliated barrier that takes weeks to settle. Do not stack it with an acid cleanser and an acid toner — pick one leave-on acid. Painful or cystic breakouts need a doctor, not a stronger exfoliant.

products.name: BHA Blackhead Power Liquid
products.whatItIs: One of the products that built COSRX's reputation, and still among the most recommended leave-on BHAs in K-beauty. It is formulated with betaine salicylate rather than salicylic acid itself — a gentler derivative Korean brands favour — in a fluid, slightly viscous base that layers under other steps without pilling. It is aimed squarely at the small, rough, closed congestion around the nose and chin rather than at inflamed spots.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin with persistent blackheads and a bumpy surface texture. Because betaine salicylate is milder than straight salicylic acid, it is a sensible first leave-on exfoliant for people who have reacted badly to stronger formulas. Dry and sensitive skin should still start slowly. Ask a doctor before using any BHA in pregnancy.
products.howToUse: Evening, on dry skin after cleansing and before serums and moisturiser. Start two nights a week and increase only if your skin stays comfortable. Daily sunscreen is non-negotiable alongside any exfoliant. Keep it away from the eye area, and give it a few minutes to settle before the next layer.
products.watchOut: It works slowly. Blackhead reduction is a matter of weeks of consistency, and the first fortnight often looks like nothing is happening — this is where most people give up or double the frequency. The "purging" explanation for early breakouts is plausible for exfoliants but frequently used to excuse ordinary irritation. If your skin is stinging and flaking, that is not purging, it is too much.

products.name: One Step Original Clear Pad
products.whatItIs: The pad that established the toner-pad format outside Korea. Each is soaked in a mildly acidic solution with betaine salicylate and willow bark, with an embossed side for a light physical sweep and a smooth side for a gentler pass. It is a leave-on product despite looking like a wipe, which is the part people miss. Convenient, well established, and one of the cheapest ways to trial a mild BHA.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and blemish-prone skin that wants a low-effort exfoliating step, and anyone who travels enough that a bottle is a nuisance. Good for the T-zone specifically. Dry and sensitive skin will usually find an acid plus a physical sweep too much across the whole face — treating just the nose and chin is the safer approach.
products.howToUse: After cleansing, sweep one pad over the areas that need it — most people do not need the full face — and let it dry before the next step. Start two or three evenings a week. Use the textured side sparingly. Follow with hydrating toner and moisturiser, and wear sunscreen daily.
products.watchOut: Pads invite over-use because they are effortless: a nightly full-face sweep, twice on a bad day, and a fortnight later the skin is tight and stinging. The embossed side is also more abrasive than it looks. There is a waste consideration too — a single-use cotton pad every night adds up, and a bottle of the same acid costs less per application.

products.name: Heartleaf Spot Pad Calming Touch
products.whatItIs: A soothing rather than exfoliating toner pad, which makes it unusual in a format dominated by acids. The essence is built on 어성초 (eoseongcho), the heartleaf extract that runs through most of Abib's range, with panthenol alongside. The pads are large, thick and generously soaked, and they are as often used laid flat on a red patch for a few minutes as swept across the face. Abib's cotton pads are noticeably better quality than most.
products.whoItSuits: Sensitive, flushed and blemish-prone skin that wants a calming step without acids, and anyone whose skin is currently unhappy from over-exfoliating. It is one of the few pads safe to use daily. If your goal is blackheads or rough texture, this is the wrong product — it contains nothing that exfoliates and is not trying to.
products.howToUse: After cleansing, sweep a pad across the face or lay it over a specific red area for three to five minutes as a mini-mask. Morning or evening, daily if you like. Pat in whatever essence remains rather than wiping it off, then continue with serum and moisturiser. In the morning, finish with sunscreen.
products.watchOut: The word "spot" in the name implies treatment, and it is not one — this soothes the look of redness for a while, it does not clear a blemish, and a persistent or painful spot is a matter for a clinician. Cost per use is high compared with decanting a calming toner onto a plain cotton pad, which achieves much the same thing for less.

products.name: Zero Pore Pad 2.0
products.whatItIs: Medicube's best-known pad and one of the biggest sellers in the Korean toner-pad category. It combines the three acid families in a soaked pad with a textured side, aimed at the visible pores and rough surface that come with oily skin. The 2.0 designation marks a reformulation of the original. Medicube's positioning is derma-tech and clinic-adjacent, which is branding rather than a regulatory category.
products.whoItSuits: Oily and combination skin with a genuinely congested T-zone that tolerates acids well. It is a strong pad by the standards of the format, so it suits people who have already used a leave-on BHA without trouble. Dry, sensitive and reactive skin should not start here — a single-acid liquid at a low frequency is a far more controllable place to begin.
products.howToUse: Evening, after cleansing, sweeping one pad over the oilier areas rather than the whole face. Start twice a week and increase only if your skin remains comfortable. Follow with a hydrating toner and moisturiser. Wear sunscreen daily. Do not use it on the same night as a retinoid or another leave-on acid.
products.watchOut: "Zero pore" is not achievable. Pore size is largely genetic and can be influenced in appearance, not eliminated, and any product promising otherwise is overselling. Combining three acid types in an effortless pad is the fastest route to over-exfoliation in the whole category — the tightness, shine and stinging that follows takes weeks to settle. Frequency discipline matters more than the formula here.

products.name: Heartleaf 77% Clear Pad
products.whatItIs: The pad version of Anua's Heartleaf 77 Toner, keeping the same heartleaf-forward positioning. It sits between the calming pads and the exfoliating ones: gentler than an acid pad, with a light clarifying edge rather than pure soothing. The pads are well soaked and the textured side gives a mild sweep. Anua's heartleaf line is coherent enough that using the oil, foam, toner and pad together is a sensible if slightly expensive routine.
products.whoItSuits: Combination and oily skin that flushes easily and wants a gentle daily clarifying step rather than acids. It suits blemish-prone skin that finds exfoliating pads too provoking. Very dry skin has little to gain here. If your main complaint is blackheads or rough texture, an acid liquid does more than any heartleaf pad will.
products.howToUse: After cleansing, sweep one pad over the face — smooth side for most skin, textured side sparingly on the T-zone. Morning or evening. Pat in the remaining essence rather than letting it evaporate, then follow with serum and moisturiser, and sunscreen in the morning. Daily use is fine given there are no acids involved.
products.watchOut: The 77% figure refers to the proportion of heartleaf water in the base, not a measure of potency, and high percentages of a mild extract do not add up to a strong product. The pads also overlap heavily with the toner from the same line — buying both is paying twice for the same formula, once with a cotton pad attached. Pick one.
